# File-type filtering in the `ignore` crate

File-type filtering (`-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`, `--type-add`, `--type-clear`)
is implemented entirely in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`, with the default type
table in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. This note covers how a type
definition is represented, how a `Types` matcher is built from a set of
definitions and selections, and how the CLI in `crates/core` drives it.

## Representing a type definition

A single file type is a `FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }`.
Multiple globs can back one name (`c` is `*.[chH]`, `*.[chH].in`, `*.cats`),
and `default_types.rs` stores the whole default table as
`DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])]` — a list of `(names, globs)` pairs
where several names can share one glob set (`bat`/`batch` both mean `*.bat`).
`TypesBuilder::add_defaults` walks that table and calls `add(name, glob)` for
every name/glob pair.

`TypesBuilder` itself holds `types: HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` (the
definitions known so far) and `selections: Vec<Selection<()>>` (the
`--type`/`--type-not` choices, in the order they were applied). `add` enforces
that a name is non-empty, not the literal string `"all"`, and consists only of
`char::is_alphanumeric` characters, returning `Error::InvalidDefinition`
otherwise — this is what stops a type name from containing a colon or comma,
which would otherwise be ambiguous with `add_def`'s own syntax.

`add_def` parses the string form contributors and end users pass to
`--type-add`. Splitting on `:` gives either two parts (`name:glob`, a normal
definition) or three parts where the middle part is literally `include`
(`name:include:other,names`). The include form is resolved *eagerly*: it looks
up each referenced type's current `globs` in `self.types` and copies them into
the new definition via repeated `add` calls. Because this happens at the
moment `add_def` runs, an include only sees types defined *so far* — a later
`--type-add` that extends one of the included types does not retroactively
widen the includer, so command-line flag order matters. Before touching
anything, `add_def` also checks that every included type name already exists,
so a bad reference fails without partially applying the good ones —
`test_invalid_defs` asserts exactly this atomicity.

`Selection<T>` (`Select(String, T)` or `Negate(String, T)`) records one
`--type`/`--type-not` choice with its target name; `TypesBuilder` stores
`Selection<()>` before a build and `Types` stores `Selection<FileTypeDef>`
after. `select("all")`/`negate("all")` expand immediately into one selection
per key currently in `self.types`, so this too is order-sensitive relative to
any `--type-add` that hasn't run yet.

## Building the matcher

`TypesBuilder::build` turns the accumulated state into a `Types`. For each
selection, in order, it resolves the referenced `FileTypeDef` (or returns
`Error::UnrecognizedFileType`) and adds every one of its globs to a single
`GlobSetBuilder`, using `GlobBuilder::new(glob).literal_separator(true)` — so a
`*` never crosses a `/`, and matching is really against a bare file name, never
a path segment. Each glob added is paired with a `glob_to_selection:
Vec<(usize, usize)>` entry recording which selection, and which glob within
that selection's definition, it came from — one flat `GlobSet` plus a side
table mapping a glob index back to its owner, rather than one `GlobSet` per
type.

`Types` also precomputes `has_selected: bool` — true if at least one
non-negated selection exists. This is what makes `--type-not py` alone act as
a blacklist while `--type py` alone acts as a whitelist.

## Matching a path

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` short-circuits to `Match::None` for directories
or an empty glob set (`dir.rs` also checks `types.is_empty()` before calling
this, to skip the cost entirely when no type filter is configured). Otherwise
it extracts the file's base name via `pathutil::file_name` — matching never
sees a full path — and calls `self.set.matches_into(name, &mut matches)`,
which appends every matching glob index into a scratch `Vec<usize>`. `matches`
comes from `Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` (`regex_automata::util::pool::Pool`), which
recycles per-thread scratch buffers so `matched` can take `&self` under
concurrent walking rather than `&mut self`.

Precedence is `matches.last()`: `GlobSet::matches_into` returns indices in
glob-set insertion order, and globs were inserted selection-by-selection in
the order the caller applied `select`/`negate`, so the *last-applied*
selection whose glob matches wins — not the most specific glob or the
lexicographically last name. If nothing matched but `has_selected` is true,
the path is `Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())` — ignored with no owning
definition, since the ignore comes from the whitelist's absence rather than an
actual negated glob. The returned `Glob<'a>` wraps either that
`UnmatchedIgnore` case or `Matched { def: &'a FileTypeDef }`, exposed via
`file_type_def()` for reporting which type/glob decided a result.

## Where it plugs into the walker and the CLI

`ignore::WalkBuilder::types` (`crates/ignore/src/walk.rs`) forwards a built
`Types` to `IgnoreBuilder::types` (`crates/ignore/src/dir.rs`), stored as
`Arc<Types>` and consulted from `Ignore::matched` only if
`!self.0.types.is_empty()`, *after* `-g/--glob` overrides and ignore-file
rules: an `Ignore` result returns immediately, a `Whitelist` result is
remembered but doesn't short-circuit, since a later ignore file could still
exclude the path. That's the source of the documented rule that `--type` has
lower precedence than `--glob` and ignore-file rules.

On the CLI side, `crates/core/flags/lowargs.rs` defines
`TypeChange { Clear { name }, Add { def }, Select { name }, Negate { name } }`,
and `LowArgs.type_changes: Vec<TypeChange>` preserves flag order exactly as
parsed. `crates/core/flags/defs.rs` implements `Flag` for `Type` (`-t`),
`TypeAdd` (`--type-add`), `TypeClear` (`--type-clear`) and `TypeNot` (`-T`),
each just pushing one `TypeChange` variant. `hiargs.rs::types` replays that
vector, in order, against one `TypesBuilder` seeded with `add_defaults()`, so
`--type-clear foo --type-add 'foo:*.foo'` clears before re-adding, while the
reverse order would not.

## Notes for a contributor working in this area

- New defaults go in `DEFAULT_TYPES`; its doc comment asks for lexicographic
  order and 79-column wrapping.
- `add`'s alphanumeric check is the only thing preventing a type name from
  colliding with `add_def`'s `:` and `,` delimiters — loosening it needs a
  matching parser change.
- Matcher tests live in `types.rs`'s `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`, driven by the
  `matched!` macro over a shared `types()` fixture; that's the place to add a
  case for a new precedence or include-resolution scenario, rather than
  testing through the CLI layer.
